rationale: A wins because it gives the founder more usable reporter lanes and better proof gates without needing to invent a whole market mood. Its best work is the contrarian line, "Oatly says its latte just got greener. It's also closing a factory and still losing money," which has a real tension an editor could assign. B has good instincts, but "customers who don't specify get oat milk" is not in the update; that is not color, that's a factual landmine.
gaps_in_A: "A 1,400-location Northeast coffee chain just made oat milk the default, not the option" overstates the fact. The update says default non-dairy option, not default milk for all customers.
"One coffee chain just made dairy optional. Dairy is taking notice." invents both the displacement framing and the dairy-industry reaction before proof exists.
The category angle admits the weakness but still stretches one deal into "whether 'default non-dairy' is becoming a real foodservice standard" without a second example.
The first, third, and fifth angles all lean on the same default-placement fact; they are differentiated, but the set is still heavy on one fragile interpretation.
gaps_in_B: "customers who don't specify get oat milk" is a major unsupported claim. Default non-dairy option does not mean the chain replaced dairy as the automatic pour.
"falling volumes, shrinking retail shelf space, canceled expansions" is invented market context. If you need those facts, go find them; don't smuggle them in as atmosphere.
"Customer-story ... no_journalist_shape" contradicts the kept first angle, which is itself a customer/operator story about the unnamed chain.
Angles three and four are too close: "Cut a factory, win the café deal" and "fewer factories and a bigger café footprint" are the same business thesis in different shoes.
